parsed.hook: Sonoma Mountain matters here because the vineyard sits above the fog line on the eastern slopes, where morning sun arrives early and the nights still cool hard. That combination gives Chardonnay more breadth than Sonoma Coast and more cut than a warm valley-floor bottling, which is exactly why this wine can carry both ripe fruit and firm structure.
parsed.wine_summary:
Paul Hobbs built his reputation on site-driven wines from California’s best ridgelines and cool, high-elevation pockets, and this Richard Dinner Cuvée Agustina Chardonnay fits that brief. Sonoma Mountain AVA is only 5,000 acres, with rocky volcanic soils, clay loam, and rocky loam on slopes ranging from 400 to 2,295 feet; those conditions push vines to dig deep and keep yields modest, which concentrates flavor and preserves acid.

For Chardonnay, that usually means orchard fruit rather than tropical overreach, plus a stony edge that reads as tension on the palate. In this bottling, the mountain site should favor citrus, white peach, and toasted nut notes over broad, buttery sweetness; the producer’s style often leans into barrel texture without flattening the wine’s line. That is what makes it useful at the table: it has enough ripeness for richer dishes, but the altitude and diurnal swing keep it from tasting sleepy.
parsed.terroir_expression: The eastern flank of Sonoma Mountain sits above the marine fog layer, so the vines get longer sun exposure than the valley floor while still cooling down sharply at night. That diurnal range slows sugar accumulation and protects acidity, which is why the wine can taste ripe without losing lift. Add volcanic bedrock, rocky loam, and clay loam, and you get a Chardonnay with mineral grip, savory density, and a finish that feels more angular than creamy.
parsed.vinification_summary: This wine is almost certainly built to balance mountain fruit with cellar texture, because Paul Hobbs commonly uses oak and lees work to shape Chardonnay without erasing site character. Lees are the spent yeast cells left after fermentation; keeping wine in contact with them can add weight and a brioche-like note while also softening the mid-palate. For a Sonoma Mountain Chardonnay, that kind of élevage makes sense: it amplifies the wine’s breadth, but the underlying acidity and rocky-soil tension should keep the oak in check rather than letting it dominate.
parsed.food_pairing:
Seared scallops with browned butter and cauliflower purée: the wine’s acidity cuts the butter, while the mountain-grown fruit stands up to the sweetness of the scallops.

Nashville hot chicken: the Chardonnay’s ripeness cools the chile heat better than a leaner white, and the oak-derived richness softens the crust’s spice.

Roast chicken with tarragon and fingerling potatoes: the wine echoes the herbs, and its texture matches the roasted skin and pan juices.

Lobster roll with warm butter, or a classic Connecticut-style roll: the wine has enough body for the lobster meat and enough acidity to keep the butter from feeling heavy.

Miso-glazed cod with shiitakes at a serious restaurant: the wine’s savory edge handles umami, and the mountain acidity keeps the glaze from turning sticky.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Kistler Sonoma Mountain Chardonnay — same mountain context and a similarly structured, site-led California Chardonnay profile.

Ramey Sonoma Coast Chardonnay — comparable for texture and oak integration, though Sonoma Mountain usually brings more volcanic grip and less marine salinity.

Kumeu River Estate Chardonnay — not California, but a useful reference for Chardonnay with real acidity, lees depth, and food flexibility.
parsed.style_profile: Dry Chardonnay with medium-full body, bright acidity, and rocky mineral drive
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2021–2025 for the best balance of fruit and freshness; the 2014–2017 wines can still show well if stored correctly. Keep bottles at 55°F with stable humidity and give the older vintages a little air before serving.
parsed.value_assessment: $45–$75 is the right range for this wine, and at that price it needs to compete with Ramey Russian River Valley Chardonnay and Kistler Sonoma Coast Chardonnay. It is worth the money if you want a mountain-grown California Chardonnay with real structure instead of soft, easy oak polish, because Sonoma Mountain gives it more shape than many wines at the same price.
parsed.market_position: This is a restaurant Chardonnay for lists that want depth without drifting into Napa-style opulence, and it belongs on retail shelves that already sell serious California whites. Collectors of producer-driven Sonoma wines will recognize the name, but it also works for drinkers who normally reach for White Burgundy and want something broader-shouldered.
parsed.insider_take: The tradeoff is simple: if you want lean, steel-framed Chardonnay, this is not your bottle. If you want a mountain Chardonnay that can handle roast chicken, lobster, or richer seafood without collapsing into oak, this is exactly the lane to buy in. Most people underrate Sonoma Mountain because they focus on Sonoma Coast, but the altitude and volcanic soils give this wine more muscle and a clearer sense of place than many flatter, more famous sites.
